transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Hearing loss genetics, for Thursday, November 26.
Let's turn to Hearing loss genetics, where we have one paper today, a review from the Lu lab in Communications Medicine on GJB2-related deafness and gene therapy.

GJB2 encodes Connexin26, and its mutations are the most common cause of nonsyndromic hearing loss. The review asks why phenotypes range so widely, from congenital deafness to late-onset progressive loss.

Drawing mainly on mouse models, the authors propose two mechanisms. Profound congenital deafness would come from disrupted cochlear development, while milder late-onset loss would come from impaired active cochlear mechanics.
That matters for therapy, because a developmental defect may close the treatment window early, while a mechanical deficit might be rescued later in life.
And the therapy picture is sobering. Preclinical Connexin26 gene therapy can restore the protein, but it hasn't yet meaningfully restored hearing.
So getting the protein back isn't getting function back. And since this review rests largely on mouse work, how well it carries over to patients with specific variants is still open.
The authors' priorities speak to that: knock-in mouse models for specific mutations and better delivery vectors, which could also clarify genotype-phenotype links for clinical variant interpretation.
The takeaway is that GJB2 deafness may involve two separate mechanisms, and gene therapy will have to restore hearing, not just Connexin26 expression, before it can help patients.

papers.title: Mechanisms and gene therapy of GJB2 related deafness
